y peptide MT1 away from the receptor’s orthosteric binding site. Once the binding site is exposed, the small-molecule agonist DCZ can bind and activate the receptor. The activated receptor transmits signals downstream via the G protein-coupled pathway, ultimately initiating reporter gene expression driven by the FUS1 p

ter gene expression driven by the FUS1 promoter. How the PAGER receptor is designed to work. The yeast cell membrane is designed to carry an hM1Dq receptor whose extracellular recognition unit is an anti-H1N1 HA nanobody (Nb), while the MT1 inhibitor is designed to keep hM1Dq blocked whenever no antigen is present. Whe

cked whenever no antigen is present. When an influenza A (H1N1) HA antigen binds the nanobody, the inhibitor is designed to be displaced from the receptor; with DCZ holding hM1Dq ready, the receptor is designed to hand the signal to the humanised Gα protein (the Saccharomyces cerevisiae Gpa1 C-terminus, last five resid

evisiae Gpa1 C-terminus, last five residues changed from KIGII to EYNLV) and then to the yeast MAPK cascade, where the FUS1 promoter drives the yEGFP or lacZ reporter. All of this is the intended design; no detection performance is claimed here. Future Vision: From Modular Research to Shared Public Health Value From Mo

ch to Shared Public Health Value From Modular Research to Shared Public Health Value EchoYeast’s contribution goes beyond the pursuit of a single biosensor. By sharing characterized reporter parts, yeast-engineering evidence, computational hypotheses, and the lessons from designs that did not yet work, we aim to give f

that did not yet work, we aim to give future teams a clearer starting point. Our long-term vision is to explore how modular living-cell sensing could support environmental monitoring—through open research, careful validation, and responsible design. Our contribution today is a documented foundation for further researc

ocumented foundation for further research. Our vision for tomorrow is more accessible, evidence-based environmental monitoring. 01 Reusable Knowledge for Future Teams We contribute FUS1-based reporter parts, yeast-editing components, and documentation of Gpa1 C-terminal engineering. Together with construction records a

ng. Together with construction records and characterization results, these resources provide starting points for future yeast-biosensor projects. Clearly distinguishing demonstrated results from unresolved questions helps others assess what can be reused and what still requires validation. 02 A Future Role in Environme

alidation. 02 A Future Role in Environmental Monitoring Our long-term goal is to explore whether yeast-based sensing could complement existing approaches to monitoring influenza-related environmental signals. Such a system would not replace clinical testing or determine whether an individual is infected. Any future app

n individual is infected. Any future application would require evidence of specificity, sensitivity, reliability, and performance in relevant sample conditions. 03 Accessibility as a Design Goal Our temperature-controlled optical-readout prototype allows us to explore how biological sensing might be paired with accessi

cal sensing might be paired with accessible instrumentation. Affordability, ease of operation, maintenance, and local resource needs remain design priorities rather than demonstrated advantages. Their practical value must be assessed alongside biological performance. 04 Open Development, Responsible Progress We aim to

lopment, Responsible Progress We aim to share not only successful modules, but also limitations—including unresolved full-length receptor expression and HA-dependent activation. Future work must address biological containment, sample handling, and the interpretation of results. By making both progress and uncertainty v
y making both progress and uncertainty visible, EchoYeast seeks to support more transparent and responsible biosensor development. Explore Our Wiki Design Results Model Human Practices

nza Signals An engineered yeast biosensor for influenza A hemagglutinin recognition and environmental surveillance Can a living cell transform an invisible antigen-recognition event into a readable response? Abstract Seasonal influenza remains a global public-health challenge. The World Health Organization estimates th

e World Health Organization estimates that seasonal influenza causes approximately one billion cases, three to five million severe cases and 290,000–650,000 respiratory deaths worldwide each year. Influenza A and influenza B viruses both contribute to seasonal epidemics, while currently circulating human influenza A vi

rrently circulating human influenza A viruses include A(H1N1)pdm09 and A(H3N2). Most established influenza testing workflows are designed around clinical or laboratory samples collected from individuals. [1] EchoYeast explores a complementary question: can an engineered living cell recognize influenza A hemagglutinin (

ll recognize influenza A hemagglutinin (HA) and convert that recognition event into a measurable biological output? EchoYeast uses Saccharomyces cerevisiae BY4741 as an engineered chassis. The project combines an HA-recognizing nanobody, an antigen-gated GPCR-inspired receptor, a humanized G-protein coupling interface,

humanized G-protein coupling interface, the yeast pheromone-response MAPK pathway and a FUS1-driven reporter system. Team Design Figure 1. Intended HA-to-reporter signaling mechanism of EchoYeast. Our current work supports the characterization of the downstream FUS1 reporter system and the construction of several chas

tem and the construction of several chassis-engineering modules, while full-length receptor expression, HA-dependent activation and integration with air sampling remain to be demonstrated. Team Results Therefore, EchoYeast is currently an engineering exploration of a modular living-cell biosensor, rather than a clinica

ng-cell biosensor, rather than a clinically validated diagnostic device or a field-deployed airborne influenza detector. Why EchoYeast? Why influenza? A recurring global health challenge Seasonal influenza affects populations worldwide and causes substantial morbidity and mortality every year. People at increased risk

ty every year. People at increased risk of severe influenza complications include older adults, young children, pregnant individuals, people with chronic diseases and people with weakened immune systems. Influenza outbreaks can also produce school absenteeism, work absenteeism and pressure on healthcare services. [1] F

d pressure on healthcare services. [1] For schools, hospitals, nursing institutions, dormitories and other shared indoor environments, we ask whether environmental information could complement individual-centered surveillance. This does not mean replacing clinical diagnosis, vaccination or established laboratory testin

ination or established laboratory testing. It means exploring whether a shared environment can provide an additional source of information about respiratory-virus risk. A global policy context The WHO Global Influenza Strategy 2019–2030 provides a framework for strengthening seasonal influenza prevention and control an

onal influenza prevention and control and preparing for future influenza pandemics. The strategy emphasizes stronger national capacities and the development of improved tools for influenza prevention, detection, control and treatment. [2] United Nations Sustainable Development Goal Target 3.d calls for strengthening th

al Target 3.d calls for strengthening the capacity of countries, particularly developing countries, for early warning, risk reduction and management of national and global health risks. [3] China’s 2024 guidance on an intelligent multi-point infectious-disease surveillance and early-warning system also calls for multip

rly-warning system also calls for multiple surveillance channels, including environmental risk-factor monitoring, together with stronger risk assessment and early-warning coordination. [4] These global and national frameworks provide the public-health context for our project, but they do not endorse EchoYeast or establ

they do not endorse EchoYeast or establish its technical performance. Why consider air and exhaled breath? Influenza-related signals can be found in exhaled particles Respiratory particles can contain influenza-related material. Yan and colleagues detected influenza viral RNA in fine and coarse aerosol fractions colle

fine and coarse aerosol fractions collected from symptomatic seasonal influenza cases. In their study, infectious virus was recovered from a proportion of validly cultured fine-aerosol samples. The study also found that coughing and sneezing were not necessary for the generation of infectious aerosols. [5] These findi

of infectious aerosols. [5] These findings support the importance of studying respiratory aerosols, but they do not prove that any environmental biosensor can provide presymptomatic diagnosis. Airborne-virus detection is an integrated engineering problem Airborne-virus detection is affected by particle size, sampling

is affected by particle size, sampling efficiency, target concentration, sample recovery and the preservation of detectable material. A sampler may process a large volume of air while collecting only a small amount of target material into the receiving liquid. [6] The performance of the complete system therefore depen

e of the complete system therefore depends on more than molecular recognition. For EchoYeast, an integrated workflow must answer four questions: Can the target be collected from air or exhaled breath? Does the collected material remain recognizable? Can molecular recognition be transmitted into the engineered yeast pat

ransmitted into the engineered yeast pathway? Can the final output be distinguished from background and nonspecific responses? We regard sampling, recognition, signal processing and readout as one connected engineering chain. Existing airborne-virus technologies Airborne-virus monitoring is already an active research f

nitoring is already an active research field. Li and colleagues developed an integrated aerosol-monitoring platform that detected multiple respiratory viruses, including influenza A, using aerosol sampling and microfluidic nucleic-acid detection. This work demonstrates the potential of integrated environmental surveill

ial of integrated environmental surveillance while also illustrating the importance of sensitivity, sample enrichment, automation and field deployment. [8] EchoYeast does not claim to outperform nucleic-acid-based systems. Instead, it explores whether an engineered living cell can provide a different route for antigen

n provide a different route for antigen recognition and signal amplification Why engineer yeast? Existing detection methods and a different design space Influenza can be detected using methods including nucleic-acid testing, antigen detection and virus isolation. [1] A systematic review and meta-analysis found that dig

review and meta-analysis found that digital immunoassays and rapid nucleic-acid amplification tests generally showed higher pooled sensitivity than traditional rapid influenza diagnostic tests, while specificity was generally high across the evaluated categories. [7] These methods are valuable, but they are generally

ds are valuable, but they are generally designed around prepared samples and dedicated testing workflows. EchoYeast explores a different design space in which recognition and signal processing are encoded within a living cell. The intended advantages of this design are modularity, genetic programmability and the possib

, genetic programmability and the possibility of connecting recognition to intracellular amplification. These are design goals rather than experimentally demonstrated advantages over existing diagnostic technologies. Yeast as a signal-processing chassis Yeast contains a native GPCR–G-protein–MAPK signaling architecture

CR–G-protein–MAPK signaling architecture that can be connected to heterologous receptors. Previous work has shown that yeast GPCR signaling can be engineered and tuned to generate measurable responses to selected extracellular stimuli. [9] We selected S. cerevisiae BY4741 as the chassis for EchoYeast and designed a mod

chassis for EchoYeast and designed a modular system containing recognition, gating, signal coupling and reporter-output layers. Team Design The central principle is: The recognition event is converted into a cellular signaling event, and the cellular signaling event is converted into a reporter output. Our design Syste

into a reporter output. Our design System architecture EchoYeast contains five connected engineering modules: HA recognition module Antigen-gated receptor module G-protein coupling module Chassis-engineering module Reporter-output module The intended architecture is shown below: Figure 2. Overall system architecture of

Figure 2. Overall system architecture of EchoYeast. This architecture is a design model. Each connection requires independent experimental validation. Team Design Team Results Module 1: HA recognition Why target the HA stem region? Influenza HA contains a relatively variable globular head and a more conserved membrane-

ular head and a more conserved membrane-proximal stem region. Gaiotto and Hufton used yeast display and deep mutational scanning to investigate cross-neutralizing nanobodies that bind a conserved pocket in the HA2 stem region. [10] The HA stem therefore provides a literature-supported starting point for exploring recog

orted starting point for exploring recognition that is not restricted to a single highly variable head epitope. Why use R1a-B6? Hufton and colleagues characterized R1a-B6 among a group of single-domain antibodies with cross-subtype neutralization activity in their experimental system. Their study also showed that antib

stem. Their study also showed that antibody valency could alter neutralization potency against some influenza subtypes. [11] We use R1a-B6 as a literature-informed HA stem-region recognition element for an H1N1 prototype design. Team Design We do not describe R1a-B6 as an H1N1-exclusive nanobody or as a universal detec

clusive nanobody or as a universal detector for all influenza A subtypes. [10] [11] Our computational pipeline prioritized R1aB6 from a group of candidate nanobody sequences for further experimental consideration. Team Model Computational prioritization does not prove that the final fusion receptor is correctly express

nal fusion receptor is correctly expressed, localized to the membrane or able to retain antigen-binding activity. The recognition module must therefore be validated at several levels: sequence integrity; protein folding; antigen binding; accessibility within the fusion receptor; antigen-dependent effects on receptor st

antigen-dependent effects on receptor state. Module 2: antigen-gated receptor design PAGER-inspired logic PAGERs are programmable antigen-gated engineered GPCRs designed to connect antigen recognition with receptor activation. Their central mechanism uses a conditional autoinhibitory domain that suppresses receptor act

tory domain that suppresses receptor activity until antigen binding relieves the inhibition. [12] EchoYeast adapts this logic to an engineered yeast chassis and uses an HA-recognition nanobody in the receptor design. Team Design Our intended receptor architecture is: Figure 3. Expected architecture of the EchoYeast HA-

pected architecture of the EchoYeast HA-gated fusion receptor. The exact behavior of this architecture must be tested experimentally because a domain that functions in one host or scaffold may not function identically after transplantation into another system. The roles of HA and DCZ In the intended OFF state, MT1 is d

DCZ In the intended OFF state, MT1 is designed to maintain hM1Dq in a low-activity state in the absence of HA. Team Design In the intended ON state, HA binding to R1a-B6 is expected to relieve MT1-mediated autoinhibition through a steric mechanism. DCZ then provides the small-molecule agonist input required to activat

lecule agonist input required to activate the de-repressed hM1Dq receptor. [12] Therefore: HA is designed to control receptor gating, while DCZ provides receptor activation. HA is not intended to function as the direct small-molecule agonist of hM1Dq. The TEV cleavage site is included as an auxiliary positive-control e

luded as an auxiliary positive-control element for testing whether removal of the inhibitory region can restore downstream activity. Team Design A TEV-induced response would not prove that HA gating works. It would only help distinguish downstream pathway failure from receptor-gating failure. Module 3: G-protein coupli

ting failure. Module 3: G-protein coupling Why humanize Gpa1? The coupling specificity of a GPCR is influenced by the C-terminal region of the Gα subunit. [13] Brown and colleagues showed that replacing the final five residues of yeast Gpa1 with mammalian Gα sequences could improve the coupling of heterologous receptor

ve the coupling of heterologous receptors to the yeast mating pathway. [14] Based on this principle, we designed a Gpa1–Gαq chimera in which the yeast Gpa1 C-terminal sequence is changed from KIGII to the human Gαq-derived sequence EYNLV. Team Design The intended purpose is to create a receptor-recognition interface wh

eate a receptor-recognition interface while retaining the yeast Gpa1 backbone and downstream yeast signaling context. Gpa1–Gαq chimera construction and characterization We constructed the Gpa1-humanization template by assembling GPA1 homology arms and the URA3 selection marker, followed by yeast transformation and colo

ollowed by yeast transformation and colony-PCR screening. Sanger sequencing confirmed that clones 12 and 17 matched the expected sequence in the target replacement region. Both strains showed reduced α-factor-induced shmoo formation and growth inhibition, while maintaining normal proliferation. When tested with the FUS

proliferation. When tested with the FUS1–yEGFP reporter, the humanized strains displayed strongly attenuated α-factor-induced fluorescence, indicating that Gpa1 humanization effectively suppressed the native α-factor–MAPK–FUS1 response and reduced potential background activation. Direct coupling between the humanized

. Direct coupling between the humanized Gpa1 chimera and hM1Dq in the complete receptor system remains to be validated. Team Results Module 4: chassis engineering FAR1 and cell-cycle arrest Yeast pheromone signaling can induce G1-phase cell-cycle arrest, and FAR1 connects pheromone signaling with cell-cycle regulation.

ne signaling with cell-cycle regulation. [15] We designed FAR1 disruption to reduce the growth-arrest component of the native mating response and to explore a chassis more suitable for sustained sensor operation. Team Design SST2 and negative regulation SST2 is a major negative regulator of Gpa1-mediated pheromone sign

egulator of Gpa1-mediated pheromone signaling in S. cerevisiae. SST2 deletion can increase pheromone sensitivity, but it may also alter background signaling and the relationship between cell growth and reporter output. [16] We therefore treated SST2 disruption as a signal-regulation hypothesis rather than assuming that

ion hypothesis rather than assuming that increased signal intensity automatically represents improved sensing performance. What our chassis data show Our project introduced four-base-pair deletions into the targeted FAR1 and SST2 loci and used colony PCR and Sanger sequencing for verification. Under the reported α-fact

verification. Under the reported α-factor conditions, the FAR1 knockout strain showed reduced growth inhibition compared with the parental strain. The FAR1/SST2 double-knockout strain showed altered growth and total-fluorescence behavior under several α-factor concentrations. Team Results Total fluorescence and fluore

am Results Total fluorescence and fluorescence normalized to optical density are not equivalent measurements. Our data show that a strain can produce higher total fluorescence without consistently producing higher fluorescence per unit biomass. FUS1–yEGFP Experimental Report Because the double-knockout experiment did n

use the double-knockout experiment did not include a same-batch FAR1-single-knockout comparator, the independent contribution of SST2 deletion cannot be directly calculated from the current dataset. FUS1–yEGFP Experimental Report The relevant engineering question is therefore not simply “which strain is brightest,” but

simply “which strain is brightest,” but: Which chassis produces a sufficiently strong, reproducible and interpretable signal while retaining acceptable growth and low background? Module 5: FUS1 reporter output Why use FUS1? FUS1 is a pheromone-induced gene associated with yeast mating and cell fusion. [17] Earlier pro

mating and cell fusion. [17] Earlier promoter studies showed that FUS1 transcription is strongly induced by mating pheromone and depends on the yeast pheromone-response pathway. The FUS1 upstream region contains pheromone-response elements that contribute to its inducible transcriptional behavior. [18] These characteri

iptional behavior. [18] These characteristics make FUS1 a suitable candidate for connecting the yeast MAPK pathway to a reporter gene. Two independent reporter routes We constructed two independent reporter routes: P_FUS1–yEGFP for fluorescence; P_FUS1–MEL1 for colorimetric output. The two reporters are parallel constr

t. The two reporters are parallel constructs rather than a single dual-reporter construct. Team Design The yEGFP route was selected because yeast-enhanced GFP has been developed as a reporter for gene expression in fungal systems, including S. cerevisiae. [19] MEL1 encodes yeast α-galactosidase, and its sequence and se

α-galactosidase, and its sequence and secretory-protein architecture have been characterized previously. [20] Reporter construction and α-factor characterization Our Registry-submission FUS1 promoter is a 435-bp fragment corresponding to the S. cerevisiae S288C chromosome III region from 71,368 to 71,802 in reference s

ion from 71,368 to 71,802 in reference sequence NC_001135.5. NCBI NC_001135.5 The complete P_FUS1–yEGFP reporter fragment used in our construction is 1,152 bp, consisting of the 435-bp FUS1 promoter region and a 717-bp yEGFP coding region. FUS1–yEGFP Experimental Report We used α-factor concentrations of 0, 0.375, 0.75

-factor concentrations of 0, 0.375, 0.75, 1.5, 3, 6, 12 and 24 μM to characterize the FUS1–yEGFP response system. Team Results The reporter system showed increasing fluorescence with increasing α-factor concentration under the reported conditions. Team Results The parental growth response also showed concentration-depe

response also showed concentration-dependent inhibition consistent with activation of the native mating pathway. Team Results These experiments support the functionality of the downstream FUS1 reporter module. They do not prove that HA can activate the upstream engineered receptor. Model-guided design Computational wo

or. Model-guided design Computational workflow EchoYeast contains several molecular interfaces that are difficult to screen experimentally one by one. We therefore used a computational pipeline that included AlphaFold2 or ColabFold structure prediction, ClusPro docking, HADDOCK refinement, PyMOL and SPICE interface ana

efinement, PyMOL and SPICE interface analysis, GROMACS molecular dynamics and MM/GBSA estimation. The modeling workflow screened 17 candidate nanobody sequences and prioritized R1aB6 for further consideration. The model also investigated two candidate gating routes involving hM1Dq and Ste2. The model proposed interface

q and Ste2. The model proposed interface residues and mutation hypotheses that can be tested experimentally. Team Model The limits of computational evidence Docking scores are not direct measurements of experimental affinity. A simulated complex is not proof of protein expression, membrane localization or functional si

, membrane localization or functional signaling in yeast. The Model page explicitly defines the computational results as predictions that have not yet been validated by wet-lab experiments. Team Model We therefore use modeling to: narrow the candidate pool; prioritize constructs; identify possible interface residues; p

identify possible interface residues; propose mutations; guide the next experimental cycle. The role of modeling in EchoYeast is to generate testable hypotheses, not to replace functional validation Design–Build–Test–Learn EchoYeast was developed through iterative Design–Build–Test–Learn (DBTL) cycles rather than a si

est–Learn (DBTL) cycles rather than a single linear workflow. The project was divided into four functional modules: chassis engineering, Gpa1 humanization, the PAGER-inspired receptor and the FUS1 reporter system. Team Engineering Design We designed the FUS1–yEGFP and FUS1–MEL1 reporter routes, FAR1/SST2 chassis modifi

eporter routes, FAR1/SST2 chassis modifications, the Gpa1–Gαq chimera, the PAGER-inspired HA-gated receptor and a temperature-controlled optical readout module. Team Design Build The designed modules were constructed through plasmid assembly, PCR-based donor construction, CRISPR–Cas9 genome editing, yeast transformatio

Cas9 genome editing, yeast transformation and reporter/hardware development. For Gpa1 humanization, the initial Gibson-assembly strategy was replaced by overlap-extension fusion PCR after sequence mutations were identified in the first donor-construction cycle. Team Engineering Team Results Test We tested the reporter

eam Results Test We tested the reporter system by α-factor induction and fluorescence measurement, evaluated engineered chassis strains through growth and fluorescence assays, verified genome-editing and Gpa1-humanization events by colony PCR and Sanger sequencing, and assessed receptor constructs using protein detecti

eceptor constructs using protein detection and HA/DCZ stimulation experiments. Team Results Learn Each cycle informed the next design. The reporter cycles established the FUS1–yEGFP route as a functional downstream output and guided subsequent reporter optimization. The chassis cycles led to a plasmid-free ΔFAR1 ΔSST2

ycles led to a plasmid-free ΔFAR1 ΔSST2 strain with enhanced α-factor-induced fluorescence. The Gpa1-humanization cycles led to correctly genotyped strains 12 and 17, which showed reduced native α-factor-induced morphology, growth inhibition and FUS1–yEGFP fluorescence. Team Engineering Team Results The receptor cycles

neering Team Results The receptor cycles revealed that expression, localization, autoinhibition and functional coupling must be optimized separately. Although the downstream reporter platform and several upstream modules have been established, the complete HA-gated receptor-to-reporter pathway remains to be validated.

porter pathway remains to be validated. Team Results From engineered cells to a detection concept Hardware development Our hardware work focuses on creating a compact environment for culturing engineered yeast and reading its optical output. The system is designed to maintain the culture at approximately 30 °C, excite

culture at approximately 30 °C, excite yEGFP at 485 nm and collect fluorescence near 528 nm. The excitation and collection paths are arranged approximately at 90° to reduce direct excitation-light interference. Team Hardware The hardware design includes a temperature-control module, a fluorescence-excitation module an

ule, a fluorescence-excitation module and a signal-acquisition module. Temperature is monitored using a PT100 sensor and MAX31865 interface, while the optical readout uses a 485-nm LED, a BPW34 photodiode, transimpedance amplification and an ADS1115 analog-to-digital converter controlled by an Arduino Nano. Team Hardwa

ntrolled by an Arduino Nano. Team Hardware The collection vessel, heated block, optical interfaces and electronic circuit were iteratively redesigned to improve component placement, optical alignment and assembly. A standard cuvette was also used during the testing stage to evaluate temperature control and optical alig

ate temperature control and optical alignment before finalizing the custom vessel. Team Hardware At this stage, the hardware demonstrates the development of incubation and optical-readout modules. It should not yet be interpreted as a completed field-deployable influenza detector. Integrating sampling with biological s

. Integrating sampling with biological sensing Airborne-virus monitoring is commonly divided into two steps: aerosol collection followed by laboratory analysis. Sampling efficiency, particle size and target recovery can strongly influence the final result. [6] EchoYeast explores whether the liquid receiving phase of an

whether the liquid receiving phase of an aerosol sampler could also serve as the environment in which engineered yeast responds to the collected material. This concept could reduce sample-transfer steps and connect sampling with biological signal generation. However, this remains an integration hypothesis rather than a

an integration hypothesis rather than a validated air-detection result. The complete workflow still requires independent evaluation of aerosol collection efficiency, target recovery, antigen preservation, sample-matrix compatibility, evaporation, foaming, nonspecific interference, optical background and waste containm

e, optical background and waste containment. Therefore, our current hardware contribution is the development of a temperature-controlled and optical-readout platform that could support future sampling integration, rather than proof that the complete sampling–response–readout workflow already functions. Human Practices

flow already functions. Human Practices and application boundaries From detection to risk information Our Human Practices work involved clinicians, disease-control professionals, regulatory personnel, synthetic-biology researchers, engineers, educators and potential users. Their feedback highlighted the importance of e

feedback highlighted the importance of effective measurement range, sampling conditions, response time, specificity, false-positive control, cost and standardization. Team Human Practices These discussions helped us refine the application position of EchoYeast. Rather than presenting the project as a general portable v

ting the project as a general portable virus detector, we define it as a platform exploring environmental or controlled-breath risk screening, not individual diagnosis. For early validation, controlled sampling conditions, such as a defined exhaled-breath setup or a controlled chamber, may be more suitable than open-ai

amber, may be more suitable than open-air environmental sampling because they allow better control of sampling variables. Team Human Practices If sampling performance, specificity, response time and reproducibility are established, the system could later be explored for environmental screening in enclosed spaces. Any e

ntal screening in enclosed spaces. Any environmental result would represent a signal associated with the sampled environment, not proof that a particular person is infected. What EchoYeast cannot currently claim At the current stage, EchoYeast cannot claim that it: detects infectious influenza virus; quantifies airborn

ious influenza virus; quantifies airborne virus concentration; diagnoses infected individuals; distinguishes all influenza A subtypes; outperforms qPCR or other established diagnostic methods; has been validated using real environmental samples; has completed the HA-to-reporter signaling chain. Motivation and Design Need EchoYeast requires a nanobody that specifically recognizes the hemagglutinin (HA) of influenza A (H1N1) virus with minimal cross-reactivity. We have 17 candidate nanobody sequences, but none of them have experimental structures in the

Therefore, the model must answer the following scientific questions: Among the 17 candidate nanobodies, which one has the optimal binding ability and specificity for H1N1 HA? Wha

ability and specificity for H1N1 HA? What is the binding mode between this nanobody and H1N1 HA? What are the key hotspot residues? To simulate the atomic trajectories of our complexes over 100 ns, GROMACS numerically integrates Newton’s equations of motion. We utilize

Newton’s equations of motion. We utilized the Leapfrog integrator, a standard and highly efficient algorithm that updates velocities and positions in an interleaved, half-step manner: Velocity update: v(t + Δt/2) = v(t − Δt/2) + (Δt/m) · F(t) Position update: r(t + Δt) = r(t) + Δt · v(t + Δt/2) Δt is the integration ti

t · v(t + Δt/2) Δt is the integration time step (typically 2 fs). Interleaved Update: velocities are updated for half-steps, while positions are advanced by full steps, allowing the algorithm to “leapfrog” over the current state. Efficiency & Stability: this method requires storing only one set of positions and velocit

ng only one set of positions and velocities at a time, drastically reducing memory usage. Crucially, as a time-reversible and symplectic integrator, it prevents numerical energy drift during long simulations. This provides the rigorous mathematical foundation for the stable RMSD and RMSF trajectories we observed in our

Problem Statement Waiting for someone to run a fever Influenza A virus (IAV) is a persistent global public-health threat

a persistent global public-health threat. WHO estimates that seasonal influenza causes around 1 billion infections, 3–5 million cases of severe illness and 290,000–650,000 respiratory deaths each year, with children, older adults and immunocompromised people carrying the heaviest burden [1]. The recognition element is a genetically encoded protein: the anti-HA nanobody is carried on a plasmid and copied along with the cell, so every yeast cell produces its own reagent and no antibody cold chain or batch comparison is needed [4]. The cell also amplifies the signal. One receptor activated by one antigen is

ne receptor activated by one antigen is turned, through the GPCR–MAPK cascade, into transcription of a large amount of fluorescent protein from the FUS1 promoter — a level of biological amplification a colour reaction cannot provide. Yeast is a natural match for this route as well: it already possesses a G-protein-coup

The output end is simpler for the same reason: yEGFP is a fluorescent protein the yeast synthesises itself, so no chromogenic substrate has

itself, so no chromogenic substrate has to be added to the sampling liquid and there is no substrate to be diluted or degraded [11]. The chassis is also a reassuring one — BY4741 is a non-pathogenic biosafety-level-1 yeast, and its auxotrophic markers add a further containment barrier, since the engineered strain cann

How We Got Here: From Wet-Cyclone Collection to a Cup of Glowing Medium This hardware began with a concrete observation. While reading up on how airborne bioaerosols are sampled, we came across th

oaerosols are sampled, we came across the wet-cyclone principle: air is spun at high speed inside a chamber, aerosol particles are driven to the wall by centrifugal force, captured by a liquid film on that wall, and end up as liquid in a collection cup. The technique exists in order to collect what is in the air and ha

der to collect what is in the air and hand it on for later analysis. We paused there. If the endpoint of collection is a cup of liquid anyway, why should that liquid only ever be water or buffer? If we replace the collection liquid with medium containing our yeast, sampling and detection can happen in the same cup. How

etection can happen in the same cup. How the process runs Following that thought, the whole process falls into eight steps: The device draws in air, and the cyclone spins airborne particles — including any influenza A virus present — into the liquid in the cup. That liquid is our engineered yeast culture, and the yeast

engineered yeast culture, and the yeast cells carry the PAGER fusion receptor on their surface, whose nanobody domain recognises the HA protein on the influenza A virion. When HA binds the nanobody, steric hindrance displaces the auto-inhibitory peptide MT1 from the hM1Dq receptor, relieving the receptor's self-inhibi

or, relieving the receptor's self-inhibition. In the presence of the agonist DCZ, which is already in the cup with the yeast before sampling starts, the de-repressed receptor activates the yeast MAPK pathway through the Gpa1–Gαq chimeric G protein, and the FUS1 promoter is switched on. FUS1 drives transcription of yEGF

ed on. FUS1 drives transcription of yEGFP, and the yeast begins to synthesise green fluorescent protein. We shine 485 nm excitation light into the sampling cup, exciting the fluorescent protein that has already been expressed. The fluorescent protein emits at 528 nm, collected by a receiver placed at 90° to the excitat

a receiver placed at 90° to the excitation path. The receiver converts the optical signal into an electrical signal, and from that signal we judge whether influenza A virus is present in this air sample. The 90° angle is not arbitrary. The excitation beam is strong and the fluorescence is weak, and their centre wavele

escence is weak, and their centre wavelengths differ by only about 43 nm. If the receiver sat on the same axis as the emitter, scattered excitation light would simply swamp the fluorescence. Turning it 90° takes the main excitation beam out of the receiver's direction, and two narrow-band filters then separate the two

rrow-band filters then separate the two wavelengths, only 43 nm apart. One more point is worth stating. DCZ sits in the same liquid as the yeast from before sampling begins, so the switch of this system is in practice thrown by HA alone: without HA the receptor stays self-inhibited and the pathway is closed, and only w

ed and the pathway is closed, and only when HA is present is that inhibition relieved. DCZ effectively presets the switch to a state in which it can be opened, and the discriminating signal comes from the antigen itself. luenza A virus. An influenza vaccine based on recombinant HA protein contains only hemagglutinin as a single antigenic protein and no viral genome, so it cannot self-replicate and is itself non-infectious [3]. The HA used in this experiment therefore does not produce the infectious characteristics of influenza A virus,

us characteristics of influenza A virus, cannot infect people and cannot make people ill. We do not handle live virus, we introduce no replication-competent viral sequences, and we introduce no virulence-related genes. For the recognition element we use an anti-HA nanobody (VHH) as the recognition domain [4], and the h

as the recognition domain [4], and the human hM1Dq receptor as the signalling core [5]. The PAGER (Programmable Antigen-gated G-protein-coupled Engineered Receptors) receptor uses an "antigen-gated de-repression" logic [6]: in the absence of HA, the MT1 auto-inhibitory peptide occupies the orthosteric site of hM1Dq and

cupies the orthosteric site of hM1Dq and holds the receptor at a low background; once HA binds the nanobody, steric hindrance relieves the MT1 inhibition, and the DCZ small molecule then activates hM1Dq [7], triggering the downstream yeast MAPK pathway and FUS1 reporter gene output. This self-inhibitory design reduces

ut. This self-inhibitory design reduces background leakage and false-positive risk [6]. For the chassis we use the non-pathogenic, laboratory-standard Saccharomyces cerevisiae BY4741. ct is carried out entirely under biosafety level 1 (BSL-1) conditions [1]. BY4741 is an internationally used laboratory chassis with a well-defined genetic background; it is naturally auxotrophic for histidine (His), leucine (Leu), methionine (Met) and uracil (Ura), cannot synthesise these four essential nutrients and

sise these four essential nutrients and must obtain them from outside [8]. The vector system, the reporter system and the plasmids used for GPA1 humanisation/knockout constructed in this study carry LEU, HIS and URA selection markers respectively, complementing the corresponding auxotrophies. auxotrophies. al histidine, leucine and methionine auxotrophies makes it a quadruple auxotroph. utrients simultaneously and at sufficient concentration do not normally exist in the natural environment, so our engineered yeast survives and proliferates mainly in specially formulated media.
